texts.preamble: K.Afsal Koya Thangal vs Food Inspector on 11 January, 2016 Author: B.Sudheendra Kumar Bench: B.Sudheendra Kumar In The High Court Of Kerala At Ernakulam Present: The Honourable Mr. Justice B.Sudheendra Kumar Monday, The 11Th Day Of January 2016/21St Pousha, 1937 Crl.Rev.Pet.No. 989 of 2003 ( ) -------------------------------- Cra 143/1996 of Sessions Court (Adhoc), Thalassery Stc 485/1990 of J.M.F.C.-I, Kannur Revision Petitioner/Appellant/2Nd Accused: -------------------------------------------------------------------- K.Afsal Koya Thangal S/O.Kunhi Koya Thangal Aged 33 Years, Kannur By Advs.Sri.V.Rajagopal Sri.K.N.Chathukutty Respondents/Complainant & State: ------------------------------------------------------- 1. Food Inspector, Kannur Circle, Kannur 2. State Represented By Public Prosecutor High Court Of Kerala, Ernakulam . R1&R2 By Public Prosecutor, Shri.R.Githesh This Criminal Revision Petition Having Been Finally Heard On 11-01-2016, The Court On The Same Day Passed The Following: B.Sudheendra Kumar, J. - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - -- - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - K.Afsal Koya Thangal vs Food Inspector on 11 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/107241525/ 1 Crl.R.P. texts.facts: The second accused in S.T. No.485 of 1990 on the files of the Court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class-1, Kannur, filed this Revision Petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 16(1)(a)(i) read with Section 7(i) and 2(ia)(m) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and Rule 5, Appendix A.05.08.01 of Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955. 2. Heard. 3. The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:- On 5.2.1990, PW2, the Food Inspector, purchased 3 packets, each packet weighing 100 gram of corriander powder from the shop of the first accused. The second accused was the person who supplied the same to the first accused. After sampling as per rules, one of the samples was sent for analysis to the Public Analyst. The Public Analyst filed Ext. P13 report stating that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for corriander powder under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1956 and therefore, the same was adulterated. Thereafter, on the request of the accused, second sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis. Ext.P23 report of the Central Food Laboratory would show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for corriander powder and therefore, it was adulterated. It was stated that the sample contained 5.6% moisture, 9.9% total ash and 2.1% ash insoluble in dilute HCL. 4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW6 were examined and Exts. P1 to P30 were marked for the prosecution. DW1 was examined and Exts.D1 and D2 were marked for the revision petitioner.
texts.arguments: 5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext. P23 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument. 6. In this case, Admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was prescribed as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act . Therefore, Ext.P23 certificate of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra). It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such K.Afsal Koya Thangal vs Food Inspector on 11 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/107241525/ 2 laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal. In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
